output.summary: KEP-2802 proposed a new optional pod spec field, spec.os.name (linux or windows), so API server admission plugins such as PodSecurity can identify a pod's target OS authoritatively. The KEP reached implemented status and stable stage.
output.rationale: Admission plugins could not reliably tell which OS a pod targets, so they could apply unnecessary security constraints or none at all. Reviewers debated using the kubernetes.io/os nodeSelector and runtimeclasses instead, but they were judged side-effects of scheduling and not a definitive source of truth. After a meeting, the group decided to add a dedicated pod spec field so API validation and defaulting can use it.

alternatives.option: Use the kubernetes.io/os nodeSelector as the OS signal
alternatives.why_not: The review noted that the nodeSelector "can be viewed as side-effect of scheduling", so the group decided not to use it.

alternatives.option: Use runtimeclasses to identify Windows pods
alternatives.why_not: Runtimeclasses translate to nodeSelectors and tolerations, and the reviewers said they wanted to avoid tying end-user OS identification to runtime class (for example, a runtime class may not exist on older clusters).

alternatives.option: Dedicated requiredOS field named differently or a separate Linux/Windows section
alternatives.why_not: The review favored a dedicated field in the pod spec with a struct for future expansion, so this shape was chosen rather than these alternatives; no source gives a stronger reason against the others.

evidence.quote: We propose to add a new field to the pod spec called os to identify the OS of the containers specified in the pod.
We've decided not to go with nodeSelector because even though it expresses the same via `kubernetes.io/os` label, it can be viewed as side-effect of scheduling.
As of now, PodSecurityAdmission plugin is the only admission plugin can leverage this field on the pod spec.
a dedicated field would presumably indicate the OS of the containers in the pod.
